messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At fifty-one, David had spent twenty-seven years in education, the last nine as principal of a suburban middle school. He was known for his steady presence, his ability to walk into a chaotic hallway and quiet it with a look. Colleagues called him unflappable. Then, eighteen months ago, during a routine physical, his doctor found something on an ultrasound. The something turned out to be a tumor wrapped around his left kidney. Surgery was scheduled quickly, the tumor was removed, and follow-up scans showed no spread. Medically, he was told he was in the clear. But David had not felt clear for a single day since.

The event itself, when he tried to deliberately recall it, felt oddly inaccessible. He could describe the facts—the date of the surgery, the name of the hospital, the surgeon’s face—but the actual texture of those hours was gone, as though a drawer had been pulled shut. Yet, without any warning, the full emotional weight of that time would crash over him. He might be standing in the school parking lot, or sitting at a red light, and suddenly his chest would tighten, his throat would close, and he would feel himself back in that pre-operative bay, the fluorescent lights humming, the cold gel on his abdomen. There was no image that accompanied these waves of fear—just the raw feeling, as though his body knew something his mind refused to hold. And sometimes, when the feeling came, he would notice his arms pressed rigidly at his sides, his legs straight and still, exactly as they had been on the gurney during the CT scan, when he had been told not to move. His body reenacted the position without his permission.

The smell of antiseptic became a landmine. A single whiff of hand sanitizer in the school nurse’s office could send him into a spiral. He had stopped walking past the local hospital on his way home, taking a three-mile detour through residential streets instead. When his annual physical came due, he canceled it twice, then simply stopped answering the phone calls from his doctor’s office. He knew this was dangerous—he was a widower, his wife having died of ovarian cancer six years earlier, and he had two adult children who worried about him constantly—but the thought of lying on another examination table, of hearing that paper crinkle beneath him, was unbearable. It was not merely unpleasant; it felt like a threat to his survival.

To manage the mounting dread, David had begun rehearsing conversations before any interaction. Before calling his daughter, he would script the exchange in his head: what she would ask, what he would say, how he would deflect her concerns. Before faculty meetings, he would practice his opening remarks five or six times, mouthing the words in his empty office. This bought him a fragile sense of control, but it also exhausted him. And despite the rehearsals, he found himself pulling away. He stopped answering texts from his oldest friend. He declined dinner invitations. He let the weekly poker game lapse. Isolation felt safer than the risk of being asked how he was doing, because he no longer knew how to answer that question truthfully.

The person he had become was unrecognizable to him. David looked in the mirror and saw a man who flinched at a hospital smell, who could not trust his own body to stay healthy, who could not rely on himself to endure a routine checkup. He had always been the one people leaned on. Now he felt like a structure with a cracked foundation. The body that had once carried him through marathons and parent-teacher conferences now felt like a traitor, capable of harboring a hidden growth, of betraying him without warning. He had come to believe that he could not count on himself to handle even ordinary life, because ordinary life was what had preceded the discovery of the tumor.

What finally brought him to seek help was a single moment in the school hallway. A student had spilled a bottle of rubbing alcohol, and the sharp, sweet smell hit David from twenty feet away. He had turned, walked into his office, closed the door, and sat in the dark for forty minutes, shaking, unable to speak to anyone. His assistant principal knocked twice. He did not answer. That night, he called a therapist listed on his insurance website. He was terrified that if he did not find a way through this, he would lose his job, his relationships, and whatever was left of himself. He was also terrified that therapy would force him to remember what he had worked so hard to forget. But he was more afraid of staying the way he was.
